name: Zadok
bio:
Zadok son of Ahitub served as one of David's priests, listed here alongside the royal officials of David's growing administration (2 Samuel 8:17).

When Absalom's rebellion forced David to flee Jerusalem, Zadok and the Levites carried the ark of the covenant out of the city with him, but David sent them back, trusting God rather than the ark itself to decide his fate: "If I find favor in the LORD's eyes, he will bring me back... But if he says, 'I am not pleased with you,' then I am ready; let him do to me whatever seems good to him" (2 Samuel 15:24-26). David asked Zadok to return to the city with his son Ahimaaz, ready to relay to David anything that could be learned there of Absalom's plans (2 Samuel 15:27-29). After Hushai's counsel defeated Ahithophel's advice to pursue David at once, Hushai brought word to Zadok and Abiathar, who sent their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan to warn David to cross the Jordan immediately (2 Samuel 17:15-22). After Absalom's death, David sent word through Zadok and Abiathar urging the elders of Judah not to be the last to bring the king back, helping to tip Judah's loyalty back to David (2 Samuel 19:11-14). Zadok remained one of David's priests through Sheba's revolt (2 Samuel 20:25). When Adonijah tried to seize the throne as David lay dying, Zadok remained loyal to David, and it was Zadok who anointed Solomon king at Gihon alongside Nathan, with the people's resounding shout of "Long live King Solomon!" ending Adonijah's bid (1 Kings 1:32-45). After David's death, Solomon removed Abiathar from the priesthood for having backed Adonijah and put Zadok in his place (1 Kings 2:35) — fulfilling, as Scripture later notes, the long-standing judgment against the house of Eli and establishing Zadok's line as Israel's priesthood for generations to come. Zadok's son Azariah served among the chief officials of Solomon's organized administration, and the roster of officials in 1 Kings 4 curiously lists both Zadok and Abiathar as "the priests," even though Abiathar had already been removed from office — likely a holdover from an earlier administrative record (1 Kings 4:2, 4).
